result.summary: Mercury tells how Pan fell in love with the Naiad Syrinx, a devotee of Diana. She fled him to the river Ladon and was changed into reeds, from which Pan made his pipes.

scenes.title: Argument of the fable
scenes.summary: A headnote summarizes the tale of Pan and Syrinx and the origin of the seven-pipe instrument.

scenes.title: Pan pursues Syrinx
scenes.summary: Mercury describes Syrinx, a virgin huntress like Diana, whom Pan spies on returning from Lycaeus. She flees to the Ladon, is turned into reeds, and Pan makes pipes from them.
scenes.stakes: Syrinx stands to lose her virginity and freedom to Pan's pursuit; Pan stands to lose his beloved.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Diana, linked to Ortygia, her birthplace tradition.

notable_quotes.reason: Pan's words on the reeds: the origin of the panpipes, pathos of lost love.

analysis.text: Like other Ovidian tales, pursuit ends in transformation: the unwilling beloved is changed and the pursuer turns loss into art.
The tale gives an aetiology for the syrinx, or panpipes, an instrument of Arcadian shepherds.

legacy.text: Debussy's solo flute piece Syrinx (1913) draws on the myth, and the story inspired many painters and poets.
The word syringe comes from Greek syrinx, meaning pipe or reed.

fun_facts.text: The panpipes are still sometimes called syrinx, and the vocal organ of birds is also named the syrinx.

language_notes.text: Hamadryads are tree nymphs bound to a single tree; Nonacris was a mountain region of Arcadia. Naiads, by contrast, belong to fresh water.
The Ortygian Goddess is Diana, called so from Ortygia, an old name linked to her birthplace Delos.
The bow contrast is compressed: Syrinx's bow was of cornel wood, Diana's of gold, the only way to tell them apart.
The speech Pan makes is cut off; Mercury is the narrator, and the text says only that he went on to repeat it.
Ladon is an Arcadian river; Lycæus is an Arcadian mountain sacred to Pan.

context_notes.text: Satyrs were woodland creatures, part man and part goat, famous for chasing nymphs.
Mercury is telling this story to Argus, whom he is lulling to sleep with talk and music.

literary_notes.text: Syrinx is likened to Diana in dress and look, which stresses her chastity and her devotion to hunting.
Pan thinks he has caught the nymph but holds only reeds, a reversal that turns his pursuit into the creation of music.
The tale explains the origin of the panpipes and why they are called syrinx.
